steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an ML paper proposing improvements to graph neural networks for catalyst discovery (on the Open Catalyst data). Motivate it from climate change, explain why simulation-based catalyst discovery is slow and where ML fits in, and summarize our contributions and gains.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:

- Catalyst discovery bottleneck: expensive DFT simulations
- Promise of machine learning
- OC20 and remaining challenges
- Our contributions (PhAST) and results

  - reduce carbon emissions of industrial processes: cement production, fertiliser synthesis

  - electrochemical reactions -> need more efficient electrocatalysts (cite)
- Bottleneck
  - finding low-cost catalysts driving reactions at high rates: open challenge
  - pipeline relies on quantum mechanical simulations, Density Functional Theory (DFT)
  - high cost limits number of candidates tested; stagnates the field
- ML
  - approximate calculations, cut time per candidate by orders of magnitude (cite)
  - sort through millions/billions of materials for experimental inquiry (cite)
- OC20 and challenges
  - Open Catalyst Project, OC20 (cite): catalyst + adsorbate pairs, relaxed energy computed with DFT from initial structure
  - recent progress (cite) but: performance not high enough; too expensive for millions of inferences; GNNs designed for general 3D material modeling, not catalysts
- Contributions
  - (1) graph construction for catalyst-adsorbate (2) physics-based atom representations (3) energy head, weighted sum of per-atom predictions (4) direct force head encouraging energy conservation
  - evaluation on OC20 + ablation
  - energy MAE down 5–42 %, compute time / 3–8 \times
  - CPU training, up to 40 \times speedups in parallel pipelines; more accessible
  - insights for future research; practical GNNs for electrocatalyst design

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
To mitigate climate change at a global scale, we need to reduce the carbon emissions of common industrial processes like cement production or fertiliser synthesis, and also to develop infrastructures that store low-carbon energy at scale so it can be re-used wherever and whenever it is needed. These processes rely on electrochemical reactions, so they need more efficient electrocatalysts to become more environmentally and economically viable.

But finding low-cost catalysts that are easy to exploit and drive electrochemical reactions at high rates is still an open challenge. Today the catalyst discovery pipeline mostly relies on expensive quantum mechanical simulations like Density Functional Theory (DFT) to approximate how the materials in the targeted chemical reaction behave. The problem is that these simulations cost a lot of computation, which limits how many candidates can be tested efficiently, and this slows down further advances in the field.

Machine learning (ML) could approximate these calculations and reduce the time needed to assess each candidate by several orders of magnitude. This could change the search for new catalysts, since it would make it possible to go through millions or even billions of possible materials to find promising candidates for experimental inquiry.

- OC20 and remaining challenges
  - Open Catalyst Project released OC20: pairs of catalyst and adsorbate, relaxed energy of the system computed with DFT from the initial structure
  - recent progress, but: not accurate enough yet; too expensive for millions of inferences; GNNs built for general 3D material modeling rather than catalyst discovery
- Our contributions
  - (1) graph construction for catalyst-adsorbate (2) richer physics-based atom representations (3) energy head, weighted sum of per-atom predictions (4) direct force prediction head encouraging energy conservation
  - OC20 evaluation + ablation; energy MAE down 5–42 %, compute time divided by 3–8 \times
  - efficient CPU training, up to 40 \times speedups; open the door to practical electrocatalyst design

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
To mitigate climate change at a global scale, we need to reduce the carbon emissions of common industrial processes like cement production or fertiliser synthesis, and also to develop infrastructures that store low-carbon energy at scale so it can be re-used wherever and whenever it is needed. These processes rely on electrochemical reactions, so they need more efficient electrocatalysts to become more environmentally and economically viable.

But finding low-cost catalysts that are easy to exploit and drive electrochemical reactions at high rates is still an open challenge. Today the catalyst discovery pipeline mostly relies on expensive quantum mechanical simulations like Density Functional Theory (DFT) to approximate how the materials in the targeted chemical reaction behave. The problem is that these simulations cost a lot of computation, which limits how many candidates can be tested efficiently, and this slows down further advances in the field.

Machine learning (ML) could approximate these calculations and reduce the time needed to assess each candidate by several orders of magnitude. This could change the search for new catalysts, since it would make it possible to go through millions or even billions of possible materials to find promising candidates for experimental inquiry.

To make it possible to use ML for catalyst discovery, the Open Catalyst Project released OC20, a large data set of pairs of catalyst and target molecule (called adsorbate), together with the relaxed energy of the resulting system, which is computed with DFT from the initial atomic structure and is a relevant metric for how good a catalyst is for a given chemical reaction. There has been recent progress, but major challenges remain. First, state-of-the-art models are not yet good enough for practical applications. Second, they still cost too much computation to allow the millions of inferences needed to explore the large space of potential catalysts. Third, the graph neural networks (GNNs) that are usually used are designed for general 3D material modeling tasks and not specifically for catalyst discovery, which is a complex task that may benefit from domain-specific architectures.

To deal with these challenges, we propose several model improvements that increase the accuracy and scalability of generic GNNs applied to catalyst discovery. Our contributions are (1) a graph construction tailored to catalyst-adsorbate modeling, (2) richer physics-based atom representations, (3) an energy head that learns a weighted sum of per-atom predictions, and (4) a direct force prediction head that encourages energy conservation. We evaluate these contributions broadly on OC20 and do a thorough ablation study. Overall, the PhAST improvements decrease energy MAE by 5–42 % and divide compute time by 3–8 \times depending on the task and model. These gains in scalability make efficient CPU training possible, with up to 40 \times speedups in highly parallelized pipelines with PhAST, so these models become much more accessible to more researchers. We also think our work gives useful insights for future research, since it uses domain-specific knowledge to improve parts of the pipeline that have not been investigated so far. In the end, the performance and scalability gains open the door to using GNNs in practice for new electrocatalyst design, which is the end goal of this line of research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
To mitigate climate change at a global scale, it is essential to reduce the carbon emissions of ubiquitous industrial processes like cement production or fertiliser synthesis, and to develop infrastructures for storing low-carbon energy at scale so that it can be re-used wherever and whenever needed. Since such processes rely on electrochemical reactions, they require more efficient electrocatalysts [1] to become environmentally and economically viable.

However, discovering easy-to-exploit, low-cost catalysts that drive electrochemical reactions at high rates remains an open challenge. Today's catalyst discovery pipeline mostly relies on expensive quantum mechanical simulations such as Density Functional Theory (DFT) to approximate the behaviour of the materials involved in the targeted chemical reaction. Unfortunately, the high computational cost of these simulations limits the number of candidates that can be efficiently tested, and consequently stalls further advances in the field.

Machine learning (ML) has the potential to approximate these calculations while reducing the time needed to assess each candidate by several orders of magnitude [2]. This could transform the search for new catalysts, making it possible to sort through millions or even billions of possible materials to identify promising candidates for experimental inquiry [2].

To enable the use of ML for catalyst discovery, the Open Catalyst Project released OC20 [3], a large data set of pairs of catalyst and target molecule (known as adsorbate), along with the relaxed energy of the resulting system—a relevant metric of how good a catalyst is for a given chemical reaction—computed with DFT from the initial atomic structure. Despite recent progress [4,5], major challenges remain. First, state-of-the-art models have not yet reached high enough performance for practical applications. Second, they are still too computationally expensive to allow the millions of inferences required to explore the large space of potential catalysts. Third, the graph neural networks (GNNs) typically used are designed for general 3D material modeling tasks rather than for catalyst discovery specifically, a complex task that may benefit from domain-specific architectures.

To address these challenges, we propose several model improvements that increase the accuracy and scalability of generic GNNs applied to catalyst discovery. Specifically, our contributions are (1) a graph construction tailored to catalyst-adsorbate modeling, (2) richer physics-based atom representations, (3) an energy head that learns a weighted sum of per-atom predictions, and (4) a direct force prediction head that encourages energy conservation. We provide a broad evaluation of these contributions on OC20 along with a thorough ablation study. Overall, the proposed PhAST improvements decrease energy MAE by 5–42 % while dividing compute time by 3–8 \times depending on the targeted task/model. These scalability gains enable efficient CPU training, with up to 40 \times speedups in highly parallelized pipelines using PhAST, making these models much more accessible to a wider community of researchers. We also believe our work offers valuable insights for future research, as it leverages domain-specific knowledge to improve parts of the pipeline that had not been investigated so far. Overall, the resulting performance and scalability gains open the door to a practical use of GNNs for new electrocatalyst design, the ultimate goal of this line of research.
